title: Pattern Recognition Playbook
summary: Mapping problem cues — keywords, constraints, data shape — to the short list of standard techniques, so an unfamiliar-looking problem gets triaged fast.

slides.markdown:
Fast interviewees aren't smarter in the moment — they're pattern-matching. A problem that mentions "kth largest" or "longest substring without repeating characters" is a coded signal pointing at one of maybe a dozen standard techniques, and recognizing the signal is most of the work.

This topic is that cue-to-technique map: which keywords, constraint sizes, and data shapes point where, how to pick between two plausible patterns, and the failure mode of forcing a memorized pattern onto a problem that doesn't fit it.

It deliberately doesn't re-teach the techniques themselves — sliding window, heaps, backtracking live in `data-structures-algorithms`. This is the triage layer that gets you to the right one fast.

Interview problems draw from a small, well-known set of techniques — two pointers, sliding window, heaps, binary search on the answer, backtracking, DP, union-find, and a handful of graph traversals. Interviewers aren't testing whether you can invent a new algorithm live; they're testing whether you recognize which known tool fits.

This reframes prep: grinding random problems teaches you specific solutions, but building a **cue-to-technique index** teaches you to triage problems you've never seen. The second skill transfers; the first mostly doesn't, which is why memorizing 300 solutions still leaves candidates stuck on problem 301 that uses a technique they've seen before dressed differently.

A rough triage order that works for most array/string problems: check if the input is sorted (two pointers, binary search), then check if it's asking for a contiguous run (sliding window), then check for "top k" or "kth" phrasing (heap), then check if it's asking for all combinations (backtracking), then check if it's an optimization over choices with overlapping subproblems (DP).

This order isn't arbitrary — it goes from cheapest-to-verify cue to most expensive, so you rule out the simple techniques before reaching for the heavy ones.

slides.sectionTitle: Constraint size as a technique filter
slides.markdown:
Before you even read the full prompt closely, the size constraint alone eliminates whole categories:

| Constraint | What it signals |
|---|---|
| n ≤ 20 | Exponential/backtracking is fine — the answer wants all combinations |
| n ≤ 1,000 | O(n²) DP or nested loops are fine |
| n ≤ 10⁵–10⁶ | Needs O(n log n) — sorting, heaps, binary search |
| n ≤ 10⁸ or streaming | Needs O(n) or better, often a single pass |

This is the fastest triage move in the whole topic: read the constraint before you read the rest of the prompt closely, and let it rule out approaches immediately. A problem with n ≤ 20 that you're about to solve with an O(n log n) greedy approach should make you suspicious you're missing that it wants every combination, not the fastest one.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading "top k" as a heap signal
slides.markdown:
"Kth largest," "top k frequent," "k closest points" — this phrasing is almost always a heap signal, specifically because it wants you to avoid fully sorting when you only need a partial order.

The tell inside the tell: if k is small relative to n, a heap of size k gives O(n log k) instead of a full O(n log n) sort. If a candidate's first instinct is "sort everything, then take the first k," that's not wrong, but naming the heap alternative and its complexity advantage is the stronger answer — it shows you noticed *why* the problem specified k rather than asking for a full ranking.

"Longest substring with...", "maximum sum subarray of size k", "smallest window containing..." — the word **contiguous** (even implied, not stated) is the sliding-window tell. It rules out approaches that would re-scan the same region repeatedly, because a window can grow and shrink incrementally instead of restarting.

The distinguishing question once you've spotted this cue: is the window **fixed size** (given explicitly, like "size k") or **variable size** (grows until a condition breaks, then shrinks)? That single fork determines the whole loop structure, and missing it is a common reason candidates write a working-but-clunky O(n²) version of what should be an O(n) window.

slides.sectionTitle: Graph-shaped input that isn't phrased as a graph
slides.markdown:
The hardest pattern-recognition case: problems about rooms, islands, word ladders, or account merging that never say the word "graph." The tell is **relationships between discrete items** — cells adjacent to each other, words one edit apart, accounts sharing an email — which is exactly what a graph models, just without the vocabulary.

Once you relabel it — "each grid cell is a node, adjacency is an edge" — the rest of the problem collapses onto known traversal techniques (BFS for shortest steps, DFS/union-find for connected groups). The skill here is translation: hearing the relationship structure underneath domain-specific words, not waiting for the prompt to say "graph" explicitly.

Some problems genuinely support two techniques, and picking between them is itself a signal. "Find the maximum sum of a subarray" supports both **sliding window** (if all values are non-negative, the window only ever needs to grow or shrink one way) and **dynamic programming** (Kadane's algorithm, which handles negative values that break the simple window invariant).

The deciding question: does the greedy/window invariant hold for *all* valid inputs, including the edge cases from constraints (negative numbers, zeros)? If a window approach's core invariant breaks under some input the constraints allow, that's your signal to fall back to DP. Naming both candidates and explaining why you picked one is stronger than silently jumping to the one you remember.

The failure mode that looks like confidence but isn't: recognizing a *surface* similarity to a problem you've solved before and forcing that technique on, even as evidence accumulates that it doesn't fit.

A concrete version: a candidate sees "pairs summing to target" and reflexively reaches for two pointers, without noticing the input isn't sorted and sorting it would break the requirement to return original indices — two pointers doesn't apply, a hash map does. The fix is a quick sanity check after picking a pattern: does every precondition the technique needs (sorted input, non-negative values, no duplicates mattering) actually hold here? If not, that's new information, not a reason to force it through anyway.

The fastest way to internalize this map is building your own version of it as you practice: every time you solve a problem, write down the exact phrase or constraint that should have tipped you off, next to the technique it pointed to. Over a few dozen problems this becomes a personalized, memorable index that's stickier than any general list — including this one.

For the techniques themselves once you've triaged which one applies, see the relevant group in `data-structures-algorithms` (two-pointers-sliding-window, heaps, graphs, dynamic-programming, and so on). For a much larger worked set of cue-to-pattern drills, `data-structures-algorithms`'s [pattern-recognition-framework](pattern-recognition-framework) goes deeper; this topic is the compact version aimed at the triage moment itself.
